chapter: Duke, Eddie Lang and other guitarists
title: Keeping up with the trend and professional jealousy
summary: He says he kept pushing from Duke on, while other musicians get jealous and overwhelmed by what they cannot do.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Just like me, now, the reason why I was well known like I was because everything that come into my head, I didn't send it back, I tried to hold it.
Let it out. To the public. Wherever I was working or playing, even for fun, I let it out. I'd play my best.
I imagine that's why I had to keep up, you know, to keep up the trend, following it like I did.
Because I kept up. From Duke on. Even when I was by myself, playing by myself in night clubs and different social functions and all that, I kept punching.
Yeah. Just like with the Spirits of Rhythm. I just kept on punching. There was no need of laying down.

You can't get nowhere laying down, but fall asleep or die. That's what I figured. What's the heck the use of me -- I play a little bit, try to play a little bit more than I'm doing now. I guess nobody can blame me for that.
You think there are other musicians that don't have that attitude?
You think they get discouraged or --
No, they don't get discouraged. They get jealous. Not jealous, but they get overwhelmed.
You mean they're intimidated by new styles?
In other words, they try to do it or they're not trying to do it, or don't know the knowledge of doing it. You know what I mean?
And that's where the jealousy comes in.
Well, if you can't do something and you've been trying a long time to try to do it and can't do it yet, that's jealousy, when you hear someone else doing it. That's where the jealousy comes in.
Right. That's what you were talking about the other day, professional jealousy.
